A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Sculptor and retain identifiable methods and experiments. All supplied pages, figures, tables, and equations support comparison. v1 has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–F are included in this assessment.

before.justification: v1 reports original PI-LLM and NeedleBench experiments comparing three language models with and without ACM tools.

after.justification: v2 retains original evaluations and adds trained M3 results, baseline comparisons, prompt experiments, attention analysis, and context-reduction measurements.

M1.justification: v1 leaves RL training as unfinished future work. v2 introduces supervised fine-tuning followed by dynamic context-aware GSPO, with conditional trajectory collection and incremental loss assignment. Its method section and Appendix F also replace embedding-based semantic search with exact matching and consolidate restoration operations into a six-tool suite.

E1.justification: Beyond PI-LLM and NeedleBench, v2 evaluates ACM on MRCR, LongBenchV2, and FRAMES, adding conversational reference resolution and broader long-context reasoning requirements. BABILong and GSM-Infinite are used for training. Appendix B additionally evaluates the M3 base model on coding, tool-use, mathematics, and general-knowledge tasks.

E2.justification: The original three-model comparisons remain. v2 Table 2 adds controlled comparisons against M3 alone and M3 implementations of BM25 RAG and MemAgent, alongside the supervised and RL Sculptor variants. Appendix B also adds Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B comparisons.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 13B M3 training and evaluation, a 20-step training limit, prompt comparisons using 50 samples per benchmark, and 128K filtering or truncation for MRCR and LongBenchV2. The retained PI-LLM table drops the two-update condition and averages over 4–256 updates, although the prose still states 2–256. Newly disclosed prompts alone do not establish changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds comparisons of generic versus task-specific prompting and tool-use patterns, supervised versus RL training stages, folded versus complete-context attention for 46 key-value pairs, and context-reduction analysis. These investigate guidance, training, mechanisms, and efficiency beyond v1's benchmark and context-length comparisons.

E5.justification: v2 adds attention-distribution statistics and a one-sample t-test reporting p < 0.001 in Section 4.3. NeedleBench's ten-run statement is retained in Appendix C.3, but v1's five-repeat PI-LLM statement disappears. Benchmark tables still lack uncertainty intervals; the statistical additions are localized.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results, including Sculptor-M3-RL accuracies of 99.4% on PI-LLM and 84.8% on NeedleBench in Table 2, plus prompt, attention, and context-reduction findings. Original NeedleBench table values and retained PI-LLM condition scores are unchanged. Claude's reported PI-LLM gain changes from 2.62 to 5.90 points because the two-update condition is excluded, not because retained scores improve.

T1.justification: v1 provides no formal training formulation. v2 Section 3.2 introduces the GSPO objective, sequence-level importance ratio, group-normalized advantage, and non-prefix context condition; Appendix E defines the reward function. These substantially formalize the newly implemented learning framework, although no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The central ACM claim remains, but RL changes from a future direction into a principal contribution. v2's abstract and contribution list claim effective dynamic-context training, learned context-management strategies, and reduced context consumption supported by broader analyses, extending v1's preliminary zero-shot evaluation claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of prompting failures, attention dilution, and the disadvantages of irreversible filtering in its RAG and MemAgent comparisons. It identifies limited benefits on LongBenchV2 and FRAMES. The computational trade-off is reinterpreted: v1 warns of increased costs from cache invalidation, whereas v2 argues that context reduction compensates for those costs.

D1.justification: Appendices C–F add exact system prompts, baseline preprocessing and retrieval settings, trajectory-collection pseudocode, reward specifications, and complete tool schemas. Table 4 supplies GSPO hyperparameters and hardware, including 200 iterations, a 1e-6 learning rate, and 128 H800 GPUs. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's brief descriptions.

R1.justification: The original related work moves to Appendix A and expands substantially. New discussions position ACM relative to sparse attention, external prompt compression, KV-cache methods, and revisable generation, including LLMLingua-2, SnapKV, and Self-Refine. GSPO also becomes an explicit methodological foundation.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes existing material extensively: related work moves to an appendix, teaching tools becomes a separate main section, and experiments are restructured around prompting, RL, attention, and cost. The contribution list, tool explanations, and limitations are substantially rewritten, with additional terminology and author-list edits.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn; v1's two result tables merge into v2 Table 1 with difference rows; and v1 Figures 2–3 are combined and restyled as v2 Figure 4. New training, prompting, attention, and context-reduction diagrams accompany additional result/configuration tables, pseudocode, and formatted prompt and schema displays.

improvement.justification: v2 turns v1's unfinished RL direction into a specified and evaluated training procedure, adds meaningful alternative-method comparisons, and tests applicability beyond the original narrow benchmarks. Its diagnostic analyses and reproducibility appendices substantially strengthen the paper. These gains outweigh material weaknesses: PI-LLM averages omit a previously reported failure condition without explanation, and the stronger speed claims lack timing measurements.
